metaDescription: Six sous vide immersion circulators compared on wattage, temperature steps, app versus dial control, clamp fit and how fast each heats a pot.
expertTake: The Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 is the sous vide machine to buy if you want strong heat, app control and a clamp that fits most pots, and the Greater Goods is the pick if you want one dial and no app. Skip sous vide entirely if you want a quick weeknight sear, because the method rewards planning, not speed.
introParagraphs: A sous vide machine is an immersion circulator: a heater, a pump and a thermostat in a slim stick that clamps to a pot. It holds water at a precise temperature, and food sealed in a bag cooks gently to that exact doneness, edge to edge, without overcooking.

The things that separate one stick from another are wattage, how finely it steps and holds temperature, how it clamps to a pot and whether you want an app. The six below run from a small, quiet stick to a high-power workhorse, and each is judged on what it adds to the same simple job.

products.name: Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 WiFi Sous Vide, 1100W
products.description:
The Precision Cooker 3.0 is the third generation of the model that launched the home category in 2014. It draws 1100 watts, connects over WiFi and uses an adjustable clamp that fits nearly any pot deep enough to meet the minimum water depth.

Wattage decides how long you wait for the bath to reach temperature, and 1100W is comfortably in the fast tier. The WiFi link lets you start a cook from the couch and check progress, which matters for long cooks. Compared with the Anova Pro in this guide it has less power but a smaller footprint, and compared with the Greater Goods it adds an app.

The Anova ecosystem has a recipe library, and parts and support are easy to find. Descale the heater with vinegar occasionally, and keep the sleeve free of mineral buildup. Keep the app in mind as a recipe source, and note that it also stores your favourite temperatures.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want app control, strong heat and a well-supported brand.
cons: Needs a pot deep enough for the minimum level

products.name: Anova Precision Cooker Pro 1200W Sous Vide
products.description:
The Pro is Anova's most powerful sous vide at 1200 watts, and the listing describes it as durable enough for a restaurant kitchen yet compact for home use. More wattage means faster heat-up and better recovery when you add cold food to a big bath.

Power matters most for large batches. A 1200W unit recovers temperature quickly after you drop in several cold bags, which keeps the cook accurate. Compared with the 3.0 it adds wattage and durability, and compared with the Mini it is far stronger.

Because it is built for heavy duty, expect a bigger body and a higher price. Keep the sleeve clean and descale periodically. Because the body is compact, it stores easily in a drawer next to the pots you will use it with.
products.bestFor: Cooks who prepare large batches and want faster heat-up and recovery.
pros: Fast recovery after adding cold food
cons: More power than most households need

products.name: Breville Joule Turbo BSV600PSS Sous Vide Machine
products.description:
The Joule Turbo adds a Turbo feature that the maker says cooks in half the time by using complex heating and circulation, plus a visual doneness guide inside the Joule app. It is a polished stainless stick with an automated cooking experience.

The app is the star. You pick a food and doneness and the Joule sets time and temperature, which suits beginners who do not want to memorise charts. Compared with the Anova 3.0 it focuses more on guidance, while the Anova focuses on hardware and clamp flexibility.

Because control runs through the app, check that your phone and network suit it. Descale the heater occasionally. Choose a big pot with a lid, and add a layer of floating balls to keep heat in and the bath clear of splashes.
products.bestFor: Beginners who want guided cooking and a faster start.
cons: Less flexible clamp than the Anova

products.name: Greater Goods Sous Vide Cooker, 1100W, Single Dial
products.description:
Greater Goods uses a single dial: twist and press to set time and temperature from 68 to 203 degrees Fahrenheit in half-degree steps, with no app or WiFi. A quiet brushless motor drives the circulation, and a switch changes between Fahrenheit and Celsius.

Simplicity is the product. No app means no accounts, no updates and no network failure, which suits cooks who just want a stick that works. Compared with the Anova 3.0 it has the same wattage but no remote control, and compared with the Wancle it has a cleaner dial design.

Half-degree steps are fine for most proteins. Clean the sleeve and descale the heater occasionally. Plan the first few cooks with simple foods such as chicken breast and eggs, which teach the timing without risk.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a simple dial and no app dependency.
pros: Single dial is easy to use

products.name: Anova Precision Cooker Mini 850W Sous Vide
products.description:
The Mini is Anova's most affordable cooker, an 850 watt app-enabled stick in a 2024 model. Its three-step process of attaching the cooker to a pot, setting time and temperature and sealing the food keeps first cooks simple.

At 850 watts it has far less power than the 1200W Pro, so heat-up is slower and large baths recover more slowly. It suits a small pot and a few portions. Compared with the 3.0 it saves money and space, and compared with the Pro it is far weaker.

Use a smaller container to help it hold temperature, and descale as needed. Use a smaller container with this unit to help it hold temperature, and cook one or two bags at a time.
products.bestFor: Small households cooking a few portions in a small pot.
pros: Lowest entry cost in the Anova range

products.name: Wancle 1100W Sous Vide Cooker, IPX7, Reservation Function
products.description:
Wancle offers 1100 watts, IPX7 waterproofing, a temperature range of 77 to 194 degrees Fahrenheit and a reservation function that delays the start. A display angled at thirty degrees makes settings easy to read from the counter, and no app is needed.

The reservation function lets you set a start time, so food sits in the bag and the bath begins heating later, a useful feature for planned dinners. Compared with the Greater Goods it adds reservation but has a narrower temperature range.

IPX7 protects against splashes, but do not submerge the top. Keep spare clamps in mind and descale periodically. Use the reservation function for dinners you can plan, and keep raw food chilled until the cook starts.
products.bestFor: Planners who want a delayed start and a readable angled display.
pros: 30 degree display is easy to read
cons: Narrower range than the Greater Goods

buyingCriteria.explanation: Wattage sets how long the bath takes to reach temperature. The Anova Pro lists 1200W, the Anova 3.0 and Greater Goods list 1100W and the Mini lists 850W. More wattage also helps recovery when you add cold bags. For a big pot or many portions, favour 1100W or more. A rough rule is that a stick needs about a minute of heating per degree for a normal pot, so a 1100W unit raising a stockpot from tap temperature to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is a half-hour wait, not a few minutes.

Accuracy and holding are the core spec. The Greater Goods steps in 0.5 degree increments from 68 to 203 degrees Fahrenheit. A good unit holds within a fraction of a degree, but cheap units drift at low temperatures. For fish and eggs, small errors show. Use a thermometer once to confirm your unit holds temperature, because a stick that reads 135 but holds 132 will cook a steak noticeably differently from the recipe.

WiFi apps let you start a cook remotely and follow progress, as on the Anova 3.0 and Joule Turbo. A dial, as on the Greater Goods, avoids accounts and updates. Choose by how you cook, and remember that an app is only useful if you will use it. Think about where the cord reaches, since a short lead forces the pot onto a spot that may be too far from the stove or too close to the edge.

An adjustable clamp, as on the Anova 3.0, fits nearly any pot deep enough to meet the minimum water depth. A shallow pot may sit below the minimum fill line, which stops the machine. Check your largest pot before buying. Apps are convenient but not forever: before you pay for a connected model, check how long the maker has supported its older units and whether the stick works without the phone.

Every circulator has a minimum and maximum fill line. Long cooks lose water to evaporation, so a lid or floating balls help. Alarms for low water, found on several listings, protect against dry running. Look at the minimum water depth stated in the manual and compare it with the pot you own, because a shallow pot makes the unit shut off or alarm.

A quiet brushless motor, like the Greater Goods, matters in an open kitchen. IPX7 on the Wancle protects against splashes. Look at how the sleeve comes apart for cleaning, since mineral scale builds up. Use a lid with a cut-out for the stick on long cooks, since steam loss is the most common reason a 48 hour cook ends with a pot that is half empty.

specDecoder.meaning: Heating power in watts. More power heats faster and recovers faster. Watts are comparable across brands, which makes them the easiest number to trust.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Anova Pro lists 1200W and the Mini lists 850W.

specDecoder.meaning: How finely you can set the target, such as half a degree. Half-degree steps are plenty for steak, though fish rewards finer control.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Greater Goods steps in 0.5 F.

specDecoder.meaning: A water protection label allowing short immersion. It covers splashes on the top. The label covers splashes, not a full dunk of the top.
A delayed start so heating begins at a set time. Delay features suit planned dinners, but keep raw food chilled until the start.
A heating strategy that shortens cook time on some foods. A faster mode may trade some evenness for speed.
specDecoder.watchFor: Joule Turbo states up to twice as fast.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat and recovery
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared wattage across the six sticks. The Anova Pro at 1200W leads, and the Mini at 850W trails. We weighted this because large baths need power. We began with wattage because it is stated on every listing and it sets how long you wait before each cook can begin.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at app, dial and extra features. The Joule Turbo leads for guidance and the Greater Goods for simplicity. The Wancle earns credit for reservation. We checked each listing for the control style, then for any extra such as reservation or turbo, and weighed those against the simple job of holding temperature.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and clamp
howWeEvaluated.description: We read for clamp design and pot depth. The Anova clamp is adjustable. Pot fit loses points when the listing is vague. Clamp and pot fit were weighted because a stick that will not sit on your pot is useless regardless of its power.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered brand support, parts and descaling. Anova and Breville are easiest. Newer brands depend on seller support. We looked at brand reach, parts and support, since a stick used weekly for years will need a clamp or a sleeve eventually.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each unit to a household, using relative tiers. The Mini is the cheapest Anova while the Pro suits heavy use. We kept cost to relative tiers, because sous vide listings move often across the year.

cards.label: App control
cards.text: The Anova 3.0, Joule Turbo and Mini use apps for remote start and monitoring. They add recipes and guidance but depend on a phone and network.

cards.label: Dial control
cards.text: The Greater Goods and Wancle use on-device controls. They are simple, with no accounts or updates.

howToChoose.note: Choose an app for remote and guided cooking and a dial for simplicity.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Guided doneness or a simple dial, a clamp that fits your pot and enough power for a normal bath. Avoid a unit that overwhelms with features.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Breville Joule Turbo suits app users, and the Greater Goods suits dial users. The Anova Mini is the cheapest way to try it.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cook large batches or often. The Anova Pro recovers fast and lasts.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cook small portions. The Mini or Wancle cost less and do the job.

maintenance.why: Mineral scale insulates the element and hurts accuracy. A soak in white vinegar and water dissolves scale in about an hour. A soft brush clears the vents.
Food residue and minerals build up on the guard. A soft cloth keeps the sleeve bright. Wipe the cord after a splash.
A loose clamp lets the unit tilt and misread water level. Tighten the clamp screw by hand and check it before every long cook. Check the sleeve for cracks.
App models fix bugs through updates. Check the app store notes before updating mid-cook. Keep the manual for the descaling mix.
Moisture damages the electronics and the cord. Coil the cord loosely and store the stick upright. Store the clamp with the stick.

faq.q: Do I need WiFi on a sous vide machine?
faq.a: No. WiFi lets you start and monitor remotely, but a dial unit like the Greater Goods does the same cooking. Most cooks start with steak and chicken breast, then move on to eggs and vegetables as they gain confidence. A second stick is rarely needed, since one unit can cook several bags at once.

1000 to 1100W suits most pots. Large batches benefit from 1200W, while 850W suits small pots. If you buy a small unit, plan to cook in a small pot, because a big pot of cold water will stress the heater. Pick the unit that fits your habits, not the one with the longest spec list.

A good unit holds within a fraction of a degree. Cheap units can drift at low temperatures, so check owner feedback. Pasteurisation depends on both temperature and time, so follow a trusted chart and never shorten the time just because the food looks done. Pasta water or a roasting tin can serve as a container if it is deep enough.

A pot deep enough to meet the minimum water line, with a lid or floating balls to cut evaporation on long cooks. Searing after the bath gives the browning that the water cannot, so keep a hot pan or a torch ready. Fresh herbs go in the bag, but add garlic late since long cooks turn it bitter.

Yes when you follow time and temperature guidance. Time grows with thickness, and poultry needs a higher temperature than steak. Pre-heating the bath while you season the food saves time, since the unit is not waiting on bags. Let the bag rest in ice water before chilling leftovers.

faq.q: Do I need a vacuum sealer?
faq.a: No. Zip bags with the water displacement method work, though a sealer helps for long cooks. Clean any mineral film from the sleeve with a soft cloth rather than a scourer, which can scratch the surface. Label bags with the time and temperature before they go in.
